Mikael Agricola
mik'a-el a-gri-kō'la
n. (Mikael Agricola, c. 1510–1557, bishop of Turku, translator of the Finnish New Testament and founder of written Finnish)
Finnish Mikael, from Hebrew Mikael, who is like God; Agricola, Latin for husbandman, a scholar's name taken for his father's calling.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Mikael Agricola was a Finnish peasant's son who studied at Wittenberg from 1536 to 1539 with a recommendation from Luther himself, came home as rector of the cathedral school at Turku, and in 1554 was made the first evangelical bishop of that see. He found a people whose language had never been printed. In 1543 he published the Abckiria, a primer and catechism that is the first book ever printed in Finnish; in 1544 a prayer book; in 1548 the Finnish New Testament, translated from the Greek with Erasmus and Luther at his elbow; and afterwards portions of the Old Testament and the liturgical books. He had to invent a written language to do it, and the orthography and much of the religious vocabulary of modern Finnish are his. He died at forty-seven on the road home from a peace embassy to Moscow. One man gave a nation its letters and its Testament in the same fourteen years. “because that every man heard them speak in his own language” (Act 2:6).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines an abecedarian as one who teaches or is learning the alphabet, and orthography as the art of writing words with the proper letters.

expand to see more

ABECEDA'RIAN, n. One who teaches the letters of the alphabet, or a learner of the letters.

ORTHOG'RAPHY, n. The art of writing words with the proper letters, according to common usage.

PRI'MER, n. A small elementary book for religious instruction, or for teaching children to read.

HUS'BANDMAN, n. A farmer; a cultivator or tiller of the ground.

Key Scripture

Act 2:6 — "Now when this was noised abroad, the multitude came together, and were confounded, because that every man heard them speak in his own language."

1Co 14:11 — "Therefore if I know not the meaning of the voice, I shall be unto him that speaketh a barbarian, and he that speaketh shall be a barbarian unto me."

Rev 14:6 — "And I saw another angel fly in the midst of heaven, having the everlasting gospel to preach unto them that dwell on the earth, and to every nation, and kindred, and tongue, and people,"

Pro 22:6 — "Train up a child in the way he should go: and when he is old, he will not depart from it."

Modern Corruption

The man who invented written Finnish in order to print a catechism in it.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Agricola is claimed in Finland as a national founder and the religious purpose of the work is sometimes handled as the period costume of a linguistic achievement. He did not set out to create a literature; he set out to put a catechism and a Testament into the hands of Finns, and the literature is what that cost.

The principle to recover is that the gospel is for every tongue by express promise, and that a tongue with no letters must therefore be given letters: “having the everlasting gospel to preach unto them that dwell on the earth, and to every nation, and kindred, and tongue, and people” (Rev 14:6). Paul states the problem Agricola faced from the hearer's side: “Therefore if I know not the meaning of the voice, I shall be unto him that speaketh a barbarian” (1Co 14:11).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek dialektos (G1258), a language; barbaros (G915), one of a strange speech.

Greek dialektos (G1258) — a language, dialect, speech; Acts 2:6.

Greek phone (G5456) — a sound, voice, tone; 1 Corinthians 14:11.

Greek glossa (G1100) — a tongue, a language; Revelation 14:6.

Hebrew chanak (H2596) — to train up, dedicate, instruct; Proverbs 22:6.

Usage

"“every man heard them speak in his own language” (Act 2:6) — the first Finnish book, 1543."

"“to every nation, and kindred, and tongue, and people” (Rev 14:6) — why an unwritten tongue had to be written."

"“Train up a child in the way he should go” (Pro 22:6) — the Abckiria was a primer and a catechism at once."
